extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Popular Science Monthly / general public interested in natural science
extracted.subtask_description: Compiling and editing short, multidisciplinary popular-science news items and notes that summarize experiments, observations, theories, and practical recommendations for a general audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Singing-flames sensitivity to inaudible vibrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Flames ('singing-flames') are sensitive to the faintest sounds if the rate of vibration is sufficiently high; they may also respond to vibrations so rapid as to be inaudible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prof. W. F. Barrett's experimental setup: coal-gas flame from a steatite jet with 0.04-inch orifice under ten inches water pressure; undisturbed flame two feet high falling to seven inches under the feeblest hiss. Using a Galton whistle, raising pitch beyond audibility produced violent agitation—each inaudible puff made the flame fall fully sixteen inches, roar, lose luminosity, and show ragged, flickering forms in a revolving mirror. Effect persisted at distances up to 20–50 feet. (Provides practical experimental parameters and observable markers for demonstrating sensitivity to high-rate/inaudible vibrations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Microscopical life-history methodology (Dallinger)
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine life-histories of minute organisms, make observations continuous so that nothing has to be inferred; use very high powers and, where needed, two observers working together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dallinger's practice: four years preparation, work with Dr. Drysdale requiring two observers; each set of observations continuous; employ very high magnifications (small spores required about 5,000× to be seen as they began to grow); select a manageable number of forms (six were chosen) and work their whole history out from origin to adult. Emphasizes avoiding inference, ensuring direct continuous observation, long-term preparation, and collaborative verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spore heat-resistance and implications for spontaneous generation
rubrics_metrics.description: Spores produced by minute organisms survived heating to very high temperatures even when adults were killed at much lower temperatures, bearing on investigations of spontaneous generation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dallinger observed that adults died at about 140° F, but spores could grow after being heated to 800° F for ten minutes. This result is explicit guidance for experimental design in debates over spontaneous generation: sterilization/heat treatments must account for highly heat-resistant spores and experiments must follow spores through germination to exclude false negatives/positives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optical demonstration of the compound nature of white light
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate that white light is composed of the spectrum colors by projecting adjacent colored circles and then overlapping them to produce white.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: William Terrill's method: arrange seven lanterns projecting circles side by side on a white screen; color each circle with stained-glass slides imitating the seven spectrum colors (adjust intensities by trial); then rotate/align the lanterns so the circles exactly overlap to obtain one white circle, proving the seven colors together make white. Notes: five properly selected colors can suffice, and even two (cobalt-blue and deep orange) will nearly do and produce a striking partial-overlap effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insect-extirpation strategies (Andrew Murray)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three principal modes for counteracting ravages of vegetable-feeding insects: rotation of cropping, destroying overwintering nidus or using toxic treatments, and (as last resort) destroying the invaders' food resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1) County or district rotation of cropping to remove the insect's special pabulum so the race dies out. 2) Burn the nidus where the insect overwinters or use substances such as Paris-green or hellebore. 3) As a last refuge, destroy the resources (e.g., crop removal) so invaders perish for want of food. Practical example: upon detection of Colorado beetle larvae in a potato field, immediately cut vines to the ground and scatter Paris-green over the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Size-of-medicinal-doses principles (Dr. John Morris)
rubrics_metrics.description: Key propositions about obtaining true physiological effects from remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1. The true physiological effect of remedies is best obtained by administering small doses frequently repeated. 2. Medicines so given are cumulative in their operation. 3. The effect of remedies is greatly increased by combination, the manner of preparation, time and mode of administration, etc. 4. Large doses often act as irritants and produce abnormal states of the blood (evidenced by narcotism, alcoholism, iodism, ergotism, bromidism, etc.). 5. More special attention should be given at the bedside to the influence of remedial agents, so greater certainty may be attained in prescriptions. (Serves as prescriptive guidance for clinicians and pharmacological practice.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Museum organization criteria (Boyd Dawkins)
rubrics_metrics.description: Museums are of high or low type depending on whether their constituent 'units' are subordinated and brought into an organic, living relationship or remain dissociated assemblages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-value museums: parts are duly subordinated to each other and brought into living relationship, making the collection useful for teaching. Low-value museums: mere assemblages of units placed side by side without organic connection; such collections are worse than useless educationally. Anti-patterns cited: random juxtaposition of plaster-casts, fossils, stuffed animals, minerals, mislabeled fragments and expensive wax facsimiles—these illustrate lack of organization and pedagogic failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection criteria for naturalists on major descriptive projects
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose workers first for recognized authority in a specialty and second for ability to complete assigned work within the allotted time; prefer local/national workers when they meet these conditions to reduce risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sir Wyville Thomson's justification for his choices on the Challenger work: selection prioritized those 'generally regarded as authorities in special branches' and those who could do the work within the allotted time. Where Englishmen fulfilled these conditions they were chosen because doing so reduced risk of losing collections sent abroad. This gives practical project-management criteria for staffing large descriptive scientific undertakings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breathing method to relieve wakefulness (Dr. John L. Cook)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce brain circulation and induce sleep by taking deep, slow inspirations to slow the heart and lessen blood flow to the brain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested rate: about twelve to fifteen deep, slow inspirations per minute. Mechanism: slower, feebler heart action reduces blood thrown into the brain, producing a quiet feeling leading to sleep. The method is simple and can be self-tried; its value is left to empirical testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gastric digestion timing and acidity observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical observations on stomach digestion times and the acidity of gastric juice under various conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported observations: in a gastrotomy patient (no salivary admixture) food remains in the stomach 3–4 hours; milk disappears in 1.5–2 hours; during the first three hours the chyme volume does not diminish then the mass is driven through the pyloric orifice within about fifteen minutes; stomach nearly always empty at four hours though hunger begins about two hours later. Mean acidity equivalent about 1.7 grain hydrochloric acid per 1,000, never <0.5 or >3.2 grammes; acidity increased by wine and alcohol, lessened by cane-sugar; gastric juice more acid during digestion and increases as digestion draws to a close. (Gives benchmarks and factors affecting gastric acidity and transit for physiological and clinical interpretation.)
